whatItDoes: Authorize up to $345 million in bonds for classrooms, laboratories, career-technology and school facilities, roofs, plumbing, heating and cooling, electrical systems, safety and disabled access, including the listed new-school and classroom projects. Property taxes on taxable property in the district would repay principal and interest. The district estimates $22 million annually, an average rate of $45 and highest rate of $45 per $100,000 of assessed value, collection through fiscal year 2056–57, and approximately $670,286,938 total repayment. These are estimates that may vary, not guaranteed tax caps or repayment amounts. Interest rates must stay within legal limits. Money must remain local and be spent on the listed facility projects. Bond proceeds cannot pay teacher or administrator salaries or other operating expenses. Independent citizen oversight and annual financial and performance audits are required. Some projects may depend on state matching funds that are not guaranteed. Approval requires 55% of votes.
yesMeans: Authorize the district to borrow up to $345 million for the listed facilities and levy property taxes to repay the bonds under these conditions.
noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.

whatItDoes: Authorize up to $236.7 million in bonds for classroom, restroom, career-technical and other school facilities, roof repairs, safety and security, and electrical, plumbing and sewer systems. Property taxes on taxable property in the district would repay principal and interest. The district estimates $14.2 million annually, an average rate of $47.46 and highest rate of $49 per $100,000 of assessed value, collection through fiscal year 2062–63, and approximately $511.36 million total repayment. These are estimates that may vary, not guaranteed tax caps or repayment amounts. Interest rates must stay within legal limits. Money must remain local and be spent on the listed facility projects. Money cannot pay teacher or administrator salaries unrelated to project oversight, or other operating expenses. Independent citizen oversight and annual financial and performance audits are required. The ballot question describes an approximate $47.50 rate. Some projects may depend on other funding; not every listed project is guaranteed. Approval requires 55% of votes.
yesMeans: Authorize the district to borrow up to $236.7 million for the listed facilities and levy property taxes to repay the bonds under these conditions.
noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.

whatItDoes: Authorize up to $86 million in bonds for school roofs, plumbing, heating and cooling, electrical systems, safety, classrooms, laboratories and career-technology facilities. Property taxes on taxable property in the district would repay principal and interest. The district estimates $6 million annually, an average rate of $20 and highest rate of $20 per $100,000 of assessed value, collection through fiscal year 2056–57, and approximately $178 million total repayment. These are estimates that may vary, not guaranteed tax caps or repayment amounts. Interest rates must stay within legal limits. Money must remain local and be spent on the listed facility projects. Bond proceeds cannot pay teacher or administrator salaries or other operating expenses. Independent citizen oversight and annual financial and performance audits are required. The district plans to maintain the current tax rate through its bond schedule; actual rates and timing may change. Some projects may need state matching funds that are not guaranteed. Approval requires 55% of votes.
yesMeans: Authorize the district to borrow up to $86 million for the listed facilities and levy property taxes to repay the bonds under these conditions.
noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.

whatItDoes: Increase each Needles City Council member’s compensation from $1 to $150 per month by amending the city charter. Reimbursement for actual and necessary official travel and expenses would remain available, and the amendment would not create other compensation or benefits beyond those allowed by the charter. The city attorney estimates $20,916 in additional annual city spending. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the increase to $150 per member per month.

whatItDoes: Add a 1% Highland sales and use tax, or $1 per $100 of taxable purchases, increasing the current combined rate from 7.75% to 8.75%. Groceries and prescription medicines remain exempt. The city estimates $6.35 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful city service, including police, fire, roads and other infrastructure; those examples are not binding earmarks. Annual independent audits are required. Collection would begin in the first calendar quarter more than 110 days after adoption, subject to the state administration agreement. The tax would continue until voters repeal it. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% local sales and use tax under these rules.
noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.

whatItDoes: Replace parts of Chino’s business-license tax with a tax on gross receipts from business conducted in the city, starting January 1, 2027 unless law requires another date. Businesses with $75,000 or less in receipts would pay $25. Above that amount, the tax would be $25 plus a category rate on receipts exceeding $75,000: $0.60 per $1,000 for general or retail businesses; $1 for contractors and services; and $1.50 for professional or advanced businesses and real-property or rental businesses. Revenue would go to the general fund for any lawful city purpose, with annual independent audits and public reporting. This taxes business activity, not residency alone. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the new business-license tax structure and its administration rules.
noMeans: Reject this replacement business-license tax ordinance; existing business-license tax provisions would remain.

parts.label: Exemptions and mixed businesses
parts.what: Federal and state tax exemptions and qualifying nonprofit, religious and government exemptions remain. State-required fees are separate. Receipts from different business categories may be reasonably allocated; if they cannot be, the highest applicable rate applies.

parts.label: Future changes
parts.what: The council could reduce, suspend, repeal or restore the tax within the approved maximum and make administrative amendments. Increasing the approved rates or expanding taxable persons or activities would require voter approval.

parts.label: Conflicting official revenue estimates
parts.what: The ordered ballot question estimates $4.8 million annually. The ordinance’s recital estimates $5.9 million. Actual collections may vary; the two official documents do not give the same estimate.

whatItDoes: Add a 1% Twentynine Palms sales and use tax, or $1 per $100 of taxable purchases, expected to begin April 1, 2027. Groceries and prescription medicines would remain exempt. The city estimates $2 million annually for local services and priorities such as emergency response, police, streets, flood and disaster response, parks and the animal shelter. Although this is a general tax, the ordinance requires spending to further its stated local-service purpose. The annual audit must check that restriction, summarize spending and make the summary public. The tax has no fixed expiration and would continue until lawfully ended. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% tax and its local-purpose and audit requirements.
noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.

whatItDoes: Add a 0.5% Ontario sales and use tax, or 50 cents per $100 of taxable purchases, in addition to current sales taxes. Collection would start April 1, 2027. The city estimates $32.5 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful city program or service, including emergency response, streets, public areas, homelessness and housing programs. Revenue would stay in Ontario. The ballot measure requires audits and spending disclosure. The tax would continue until repealed by voters. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the additional 0.5% local sales and use tax.
noMeans: Do not add this proposed 0.5% tax.

whatItDoes: Extend San Bernardino County’s existing 0.5% transportation sales tax beginning April 1, 2040, after the current authorization ends March 31, 2040. This would not immediately increase the rate. The question estimates $250 million annually for the adopted road, highway, transit and transportation-technology plan. Revenue would stay under local control and be limited to transportation purposes, with audits, spending disclosure and independent taxpayer oversight. The extension has no fixed end; repeal requires a countywide voter decision and satisfaction of outstanding bond and contractual obligations. Approval requires a two-thirds vote.
yesMeans: Extend the existing 0.5% transportation tax from April 2040 under the new spending plan and oversight rules.
noMeans: Do not approve this extension; the current authorization would still run through March 31, 2040.

parts.label: How the money would be divided
parts.what: After state collection fees, 3% is designated for interregional mobility, and 1% of net revenue for the administration fund. Remaining revenue is returned to the county’s subareas. In the Valley, 25% goes to local mobility, 50% regional mobility and 25% operations. In the Mountain and Desert subareas, the shares are 70%, 20% and 10%; additional transit operations may be funded from local mobility for unmet needs. Valley local shares use population; Mountain and Desert local shares use half population and half tax generation. Each jurisdiction reserves 5% of its local allocation for active transportation. After at least ten years, a jurisdiction may release that reserve if its governing body finds it unnecessary and the authority board approves.

parts.label: Spending and borrowing limits
parts.what: Tax-administration salaries and benefits cannot exceed the administration fund, which receives 1% of annual net tax revenue. Existing transportation funding must be maintained against the fiscal 2038–39 baseline, and this tax cannot replace development’s required fair share. The authority may borrow against future tax revenue, including before the extension begins, subject to the ordinance and its debt policy; outstanding principal cannot exceed estimated tax proceeds. Authority audits are biennial and local recipients’ audits annual.

parts.label: Changing the plan
parts.what: Plan changes cannot take effect before 2050. Reviews are required at least every ten years afterward, with public and local-jurisdiction input; amendments take effect 45 days after written notice to local jurisdictions and the county board. Changing subarea boundaries requires unanimous agreement of affected local jurisdictions. The measure also adjusts the constitutional spending limit by projected tax revenue.

whatItDoes: Add a 1% Chino Hills sales and use tax, increasing the current combined rate from 7.75% to 8.75%. The city estimates $11.5 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful city purpose, including public safety, wildfire preparation, open space, parks and streets. Groceries, prescription medicines, tuition, rent, utilities and generally labor and services would remain exempt. Collection would begin in the first calendar quarter more than 110 days after adoption, subject to state administration arrangements. The tax would continue until voters repeal it; the council could suspend all or part. Independent annual audits and public spending reports are required. Rate increases and expansion to new taxable transactions require voter approval. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% local sales and use tax under these rules.
noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.

whatItDoes: Increase Needles’ tax on hotel, motel, recreational-vehicle and short-term lodging stays of 30 days or less from 10% to 12% on January 1, 2027, 13% on January 1, 2029 and 14% on January 1, 2030. Guests pay the tax and lodging operators collect it. The city estimates additional annual revenue of $200,000 at 12%, $300,000 at 13% and $400,000 at 14%, for its general fund and any lawful city purpose. The measure also updates monthly remittance and delinquency rules and requires annual public disclosure. It has no fixed expiration and would continue until ended by voters. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the phased lodging-tax increase and related collection rules.
noMeans: Keep the current 10% lodging-tax rate rather than adopting this increase.

whatItDoes: Authorize up to $11.2 million in Needles bonds for roads, streets and potholes, community safety, parks and recreation, and downtown Main Street improvements. Property taxes would repay principal and interest. The city estimates $739,971 annually, an average and highest rate of $60 per $100,000 of assessed value, and $25.16 million total repayment. These projections may vary and are not binding caps. Interest must stay within legal limits. Money must stay in Needles and cannot pay employee salaries or routine operating expenses. Annual financial and performance audits, independent citizen oversight, separate accounts and public reports are required. Approval requires a two-thirds vote.
yesMeans: Authorize the city to borrow up to $11.2 million for these improvements and levy property taxes to repay the bonds.
noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.

parts.label: Conflicting projected tax dates
parts.what: The official tax statement projects final tax collection in fiscal 2058–59, but also projects its highest rate through 2060–61. These inconsistent dates are estimates; taxes would be collected as needed while the bonds remain outstanding.

whatItDoes: Revise Upland’s business-license tax starting January 1, 2027, with lower transition rates in 2027 and full rates in 2028. The first $100,000 of annual gross receipts would be subject only to a $75 minimum; receipts above that threshold would use rates based on business type. Self-storage facilities would also pay a per-unit amount. The schedule has an initial $28,000 annual maximum, with inflation adjustments described below. The city estimates $3.3 million total annual revenue, about $2.1 million more than the current tax, for general city services. Independent audits and public spending disclosure are required. This taxes businesses, including businesses operated by residents, rather than residency alone. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the revised business-license tax, transition rates, limits and exemptions.
noMeans: Reject this proposed tax revision and keep the current business-license tax structure.

parts.label: Rates and inflation adjustments
parts.what: In 2027, rates on receipts above $100,000 would be 0.060% for retail and general commercial businesses, 0.100% for contractors, 0.125% for rentals and 0.090% for general or professional services. From 2028, the rates would be 0.065%, 0.150%, 0.200% and 0.125%, respectively. Self-storage facilities would also pay $50 per unit. The $75 minimum, $28,000 maximum and $50 per-unit amount would each rise with the applicable Consumer Price Index every January 1. The ordinance retains a separate tonnage-based tax for rock, sand and gravel extraction.

parts.label: Exemptions and veterans
parts.what: Businesses exempt under federal or state law remain exempt. An approved special-event vendor without a fixed city business or other city business activity may be exempt. Qualifying honorably discharged veterans unable to earn a livelihood through manual labor may obtain a free license with the required California voter eligibility and recent medical proof. Other honorably discharged veterans receive an application-fee waiver and a $100,000 gross-receipts credit, or the specified $108 business-tax credit, with proof of discharge. State-required fees cannot be waived.

parts.label: Future changes
parts.what: The council may amend or repeal the ordinance or reduce and later restore taxes within voter-approved limits. Increasing approved maximum rates or changing the tax method to increase the tax requires voter approval. The ballot question describes the tax as continuing until ended by voters; it has no fixed expiration.

whatItDoes: Add a 1% Grand Terrace sales and use tax. The city estimates $1.2 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful general city purpose, including police and emergency response. Groceries and prescription medicines remain exempt. Collection would begin in the first calendar quarter more than 110 days after adoption, subject to state administration arrangements. An advisory committee would review tax revenue, spending and annual audit reports and submit at least one written report a year to the council. Independent annual audits and public disclosure are required. The tax would continue until voters repeal it. The council could make administrative amendments, but a tax increase requires voter approval. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% local tax and its oversight requirements.
noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.

whatItDoes: Change Colton’s city treasurer from an elected to an appointed office beginning November 7, 2028, or earlier if the current office becomes vacant. The current elected term would otherwise continue until that date. The council would appoint the treasurer, who would serve at its pleasure and would not have to be a city resident or registered voter. The council could delegate appointment authority to the city manager by ordinance. Later amendment or repeal of this measure would require voter approval. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve an appointed city treasurer under this transition and appointment process.
noMeans: Keep the city treasurer as an elected office.

whatItDoes: Add a 1% Adelanto sales and use tax beginning April 1, 2027. The city estimates $3 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful municipal purpose, including streets, emergency services, public safety, parks, homelessness response and infrastructure. The tax applies to taxable purchases by residents and visitors; transactions exempt under existing law remain exempt. A transaction would pay the sales or use tax once, not both. Annual independent accountant audits must be reported publicly and posted on the city website. The tax has no fixed expiration and would continue until lawfully ended. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% local sales and use tax and its audit requirements.
noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.
